extracted.intended_audience: students and researchers in mathematical logic, proof theory, and theoretical computer science
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and desirable properties for proof calculi, proof-theoretic methods, and related analyses (e.g., cut-elimination, subformula property, ordinal analysis, reversals in reverse mathematics). The page surveys what makes a proof system or proof-theoretic method syntactically and semantically well-behaved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyticity (notion of an analytic proof)
rubrics_metrics.description: A good family of properties for proof calculi is analyticity; the notion of an analytic proof was introduced by Gentzen for the sequent calculus, where he proved that the sequent calculus of classical and intuitionistic logics are cut-free.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyticity is an umbrella notion often expressed via specific properties such as cut-elimination and the subformula property. Analytic proofs support results like Gentzen's midsequent theorem, the Craig interpolation theorem, and Herbrand's theorem. Different calculi (sequent calculus, natural deduction, proof nets) have corresponding notions of analytic/normal proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cut-elimination property
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof calculus has the cut-elimination property if it has the cut rule, but any provable sequent is provable without the cut rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cut-elimination is a central syntactic property: from it follow the midsequent theorem, Craig interpolation, and Herbrand's theorem. Showing cut-elimination (or admissibility of cut) is a major criterion for the syntactic quality of a proof system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subformula property
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof has the subformula property if every formula in it is a subformula of its endsequent; a proof calculus has the subformula property if all its provable sequents can be proved by a proof with the subformula property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In most calculi the subformula property follows from cut-elimination, though not necessarily vice versa. A calculus with the subformula property is consistent, since the empty sequent could not be a subformula of any premise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency (syntactic)
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof calculus is consistent in that it does not derive absurdity (e.g., the empty sequent is not derivable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistency is often a corollary of other syntactic properties such as the subformula property or the admissibility of cut. Demonstrating syntactic consistency is a basic standard for a well-behaved proof system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normalisation / normal forms (analytic proofs in natural deduction)
rubrics_metrics.description: In natural deduction, analytic proofs are the normal forms: proofs that have been normalized so that certain detours (maximal formulas) are eliminated; this notion is related to normal form in term rewriting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normalization shows that maximal formulas introduced then eliminated can be removed; normalization corresponds to beta-reduction via the Curry–Howard correspondence and is a measure of the syntactic neatness of proofs. Prawitz's work formalizes this notion for natural deduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmony (introduction/elimination rule balance)
rubrics_metrics.description: In a natural deduction system, each logical connective has a pair of rules: introduction and elimination. The pair is in harmony if maximal formulas can be eliminated by normalizing the proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Harmony ensures that introduction rules do not give more power than justified by elimination rules (and vice versa). Maximal formulas act like lemmas—helpful but not necessary—and a normalized proof should only introduce connectives and not eliminate them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Locality of inference rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain inference rules are local, which is a desired property; a rule is local if its correct application can be checked by looking at a bounded (local) portion of the sequent/proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-local rules (example: the '!' rule in linear logic) require checking an unbounded number of formulas (e.g., that many formulas have ! as their outermost connective), making them harder to check and reason about. Locality is preferred for implementability and decidability considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focused proofs / focused form
rubrics_metrics.description: Focused proofs are a family of analytic proofs characterising goal-directed proof-search procedures; the ability to transform a proof system into a focused form indicates good syntactic quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focused form captures a large family of goal-directed proof-search methods. Transformability into a focused form is analogous to admissibility of cut as a measure of syntactic discipline and is useful for proof search and automation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissibility of cut
rubrics_metrics.description: Admissibility of the cut rule (i.e., cuts are not needed to prove anything the system can already prove) is a syntactic property showing the system's consistency and well-behavedness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Admissibility of cut is often established by showing cut-elimination; it functions as a key benchmark for the syntactic robustness of a calculus and underpins many metatheoretic results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representability in standard calculi (Hilbert/natural deduction/sequent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Most logics of interest can be given complete axiomatic formalizations in Hilbert calculi, natural deduction calculi, or sequent calculi; being presentable in one of these styles is part of a logic's amenability to proof-theoretic study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The three styles (Hilbert, natural deduction, sequent) are the most well-known and each can formalize propositional or predicate logic (classical/intuitionistic), many modal logics, and many substructural logics. A logic that resists representation in these calculi is unusual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordinal analysis (as a measure of infinitary content and consistency strength)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinal analysis provides combinatorial consistency proofs for subsystems of arithmetic, analysis, and set theory by associating well-founded transfinite ordinals to the infinitary content of a theory's consistency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ordinal analysis measures the infinitary content of consistency statements: for a recursively axiomatized theory T, proving in finitary arithmetic that well-foundedness of a certain ordinal implies consistency of T. Consequences include relative consistency results, combinatorial independence results, and classifications of provably total recursive functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional interpretations (constructive reduction and extraction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Functional interpretations interpret non-constructive (classical) theories in functional (often quantifier-free) theories, typically by first reducing a classical theory to an intuitionistic one, then to a theory of functionals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good functional interpretations yield reductions of infinitary to finitary theories and permit extraction of constructive information from proofs: recursive functions provably total in the original theory correspond to terms in the target theory. Examples include Gödel's Dialectica interpretation and applications to ordinal analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provability logic capturing derivability conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Provability logic is a modal logic where the box operator is interpreted as 'it is provable that'; basic axioms mirror the Hilbert–Bernays derivability conditions and Löb's theorem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A successful provability logic (e.g., GL for Peano Arithmetic) should capture the propositional theory of provability in the target formal theory and ideally be complete with respect to that theory (Solovay's theorem shows GL is complete for PA). Such completeness yields decidability and a faithful propositional account of provability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reverse mathematics method (reversal proofs and base system methodology)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reverse mathematics seeks to determine which axioms are required to prove theorems: for a theorem T one shows (1) T is provable from some stronger system S, and (2) a reversal showing T implies S (carried out in the weak base system).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The two-proof methodology (proof from S and reversal in the base system) is a defining procedural requirement. The field relies on a chosen weak base theory and the classification of many theorems relative to the 'Big Five' subsystems (RCA_0, WKL_0, ACA_0, ATR_0, Π1^1-CA_0). Deviations (theorems not fitting the Big Five) are active research targets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal proof checkability (formal vs informal proof distinction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal proofs are fully formalised and can be checked automatically (e.g., in interactive theorem proving); informal proofs are high-level mathematical practice sketches that require peer review and may contain errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For absolute certainty and machine verification, formal proofs are preferred because they are checkable automatically. Informal proofs are practical for human mathematics but may hide gaps; the trade-off between readability and machine-checkability is a normative consideration in proof development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of analytic tableau for decision/semi-decision procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Analytic tableau methods apply the central idea of analytic proofs to provide decision procedures and semi-decision procedures for a wide range of logics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tableau systems that respect analyticity/subformula constraints are useful for automated reasoning; designing tableau systems to preserve analyticity helps ensure termination/decidability properties where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compatibility with Curry–Howard correspondence (type-theoretic connections)
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof calculus's structural behaviour and normalization properties should align with the Curry–Howard correspondence, which relates proof normalization to computation (beta-reduction in typed lambda calculus).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compatibility gives semantic and computational interpretations (e.g., connections to intuitionistic type theory and cartesian closed categories), supports extraction of programs from proofs, and indicates deeper structural quality of the proof system.
